english: intend to V / plan to V
formNote: Use this to announce your own intention or a not-yet-fixed plan: the verb 하다 at the end literally means you are 'trying to / setting out to' do the verb. Form it by adding 려고 after a vowel stem (가다 -> 가려고 해요) and 으려고 after a consonant stem (먹다 -> 먹으려고 해요), then attach 해요. Sharp contrast: -(으)려고 해요 is a leaning or wish, softer and less committed than -(으)ㄹ 거예요, which is a settled decision; '내일 자려고 해요' = 'I'm thinking of sleeping early' whereas '내일 잘 거예요' = 'I will sleep early.' English-speaker pitfall: this is for the speaker's mind, so do not use it to report what someone else firmly will do, and never bolt a noun onto it — say '공부하려고 해요', not '공부 하려고 해요'.
usage: Future leaning, softer than 배울 거예요.
Stem 쉬- ends in a vowel, so no 으.
examples: I intend to meet a friend this weekend.
Adds a time word and 를 object.
올해는 꼭 한국어를 끝까지 배우려고 해요.
This year I really intend to learn Korean to the end.
Real resolution with 꼭 and 끝까지.
mistakes: 다른 사람이 가려고 해요.
This describes the speaker's own intention, so using it to assert someone else's firm plan sounds off; for a third person's stated intention prefer 가려고 한대요 or just 갈 거래요.
Keep -(으)려고 해요 for I / we; report others with -(ㄴ/는)대요.
공부 하려고 해요.
공부하다 is one verb, so splitting it is wrong; the 하 belongs to 공부하다, not to the pattern.
Write it joined: 공부하려고 해요.

formNote: This is the gentlest everyday way to ask a favor of someone you don't know well: 주다 ('do it for me') becomes honorific 주시다, and the -겠- adds a tentative 'would you mind' softness that a flat 주세요 lacks. Build the 아/어 form (도와 from 돕다, 열어 from 열다, 말해 from 말하다), then add 주시겠어요. Contrast: 주세요 is a clear polite request ('please do X'), while 주시겠어요? is a deferential question ('might I ask you to X?') — perfect for staff, strangers, or anyone senior; 줄래? in the casual tab is only for close friends. Pitfall: English speakers often forget the 아/어 link and say '돕아 주시겠어요' — the verb 돕다 is ㅂ-irregular, so it must be 도와 주시겠어요.
usage: Could you please say that again?
examples: Could you help me with this?
Could you open the window for me?
Sorry, but could you speak slowly?
mistakes: 돕아 주시겠어요?
돕다 is a ㅂ-irregular verb, so the 아/어 form is 도와, not 돕아.
Say 도와 주시겠어요? (or written together, 도와주시겠어요?).
열어 주시겠어요 (said to a close friend).
The 주시- honorific is too formal for a buddy; among friends it sounds stiff.
Use the casual tab: 열어 줄래?

english: it is good to V / you should V
formNote: This gives gentle, non-pushy advice — literally 'doing V is good' — so it lands much softer than a direct order. Attach 는 게 좋아요 to the dictionary stem (가다 -> 가는 게 좋아요); ㄹ-stems drop the ㄹ before 는, so 만들다 -> 만드는 게 좋아요 and 살다 -> 사는 게 좋아요. The 게 here is a contraction of 것이 ('the thing of doing X'). Sharp contrast: 는 게 좋아요 is a friendly recommendation, whereas -아/어야 해요 is an obligation you cannot skip; '쉬는 게 좋아요' = 'you'd be better off resting' but '쉬어야 해요' = 'you have to rest.' Pitfall: don't write the past 'V은 게 좋아요' for advice — advice about an action you should take always uses the present 는 게, since you're recommending it now.
usage: ㄹ-stem 만들다 drops ㄹ before 는.
examples: 감기에는 물을 많이 마시는 게 좋아요.
For a cold it's good to drink lots of water.
시험이 있으니까 오늘은 일찍 자는 게 좋아요.
Since you have a test, today it'd be best to sleep early.
mistakes: 가는 것이 좋아요 written as 가는 거이 좋아요.
The contraction of 것이 is 게, never 거이; 거이 is not a real form.
Use 게: 가는 게 좋아요.
만들는 게 좋아요.
ㄹ-stem verbs drop the ㄹ before 는, so 만들다 becomes 만드는.
Say 만드는 게 좋아요.

english: I think it will / it seems
formNote: Use this to make a soft prediction or guess about something not yet certain — literally 'it seems like the thing that will happen.' Add ㄹ 것 같아요 after a vowel stem (오다 -> 올 것 같아요) and 을 것 같아요 after a consonant stem (늦다 -> 늦을 것 같아요); 같다 means 'to be like / seem.' Important contrast inside this same pattern: the -(으)ㄹ form is a guess about the future or the uncertain ('비가 올 것 같아요' = 'it looks like it'll rain'), while -는 것 같아요 guesses about right now ('비가 오는 것 같아요' = 'it seems to be raining') and -(으)ㄴ 것 같아요 guesses about the past ('비가 온 것 같아요' = 'it seems it rained'). Pitfall: English 'I think' is often a firm opinion, but -(으)ㄹ 것 같아요 is deliberately tentative and polite, so don't use it when you actually know — for certainty use -(으)ㄹ 거예요.
usage: It looks like it'll be tasty.
Soft opinion, not a firm claim.
examples: 길이 막혀서 좀 늦을 것 같아요.
Traffic's heavy, so I'll be a bit late.
이 영화 평이 좋던데 재미있을 것 같아요.
The reviews were good, so I think this movie will be fun.
mistakes: 비가 올 거 같아요 used to state a known fact.
This pattern signals a guess, so using it when you are certain confuses the listener about how sure you are.
If you know for sure, drop the guess: 비가 올 거예요.
비가 오는 것 같아요 to mean 'it'll rain later.'
는 것 같아요 guesses about the present (it seems to be raining now); future needs 올.
For a future guess use 올 것 같아요.

formNote: This is the 'have you ever...' experience pattern: 적 is a bound noun meaning 'a (past) occasion,' so the whole thing literally says 'there exists an occasion on which I did V.' Add ㄴ 적이 있어요 after a vowel stem (가다 -> 간 적이 있어요) and 은 적이 있어요 after a consonant stem (먹다 -> 먹은 적이 있어요); swap 있어요 for 없어요 to say you never have. Sharp contrast with plain past tense: -았/었어요 just reports that something happened ('어제 갔어요' = 'I went yesterday'), while -(으)ㄴ 적이 있어요 highlights it as a life experience worth noting ('가 본 적이 있어요' = 'I've had the experience of going'), so it pairs naturally with -아/어 보다 ('try'). Pitfall: don't use it for a recent or one-time event you'd describe with a date — 'I ate breakfast this morning' is 아침을 먹었어요, not 먹은 적이 있어요.
usage: Pairs with 보다 'try': 가 보다 -> 가 본.
examples: Have you ever watched a Korean movie?
저는 직접 김치를 만든 적은 없지만 먹어 본 적은 많아요.
I've never made kimchi myself, but I've eaten it many times.
Contrastive 은 marks experience vs none.
mistakes: 오늘 아침에 밥을 먹은 적이 있어요.
A dated one-time event is plain past tense, not life experience; the pattern is reserved for 'ever in your life' situations.
Say 오늘 아침에 밥을 먹었어요.
간 적이 안 있어요.
The negative of 있다 is 없다, so you cannot use 안 with it here.
Use 없어요: 간 적이 없어요.

formNote: Use this to name a noun as the cause of something, usually a result you didn't choose — it leans toward blame or unwanted consequences. Place the noun directly before 때문에 with no particle (비 때문에, 일 때문에). Sharp contrast: 때문에 most often introduces a negative cause ('비 때문에 취소했어요' = 'I canceled because of the rain'), whereas 덕분에 ('thanks to') introduces a positive cause you're grateful for ('친구 덕분에 잘 끝났어요'), so swapping them changes the whole tone. Also note 때문에 takes a NOUN; to give a verb/adjective reason you must say -기 때문에 (바쁘기 때문에). Pitfall: English 'because' is one word that handles both, but Korean splits noun-cause (때문에) from clause-cause (-아서 / -니까 / -기 때문에), and learners wrongly insert a particle — it's 비 때문에, never 비가 때문에.
examples: I canceled the plan because of the rain.
These days I'm so busy because of work.
감기 때문에 어제 학교에 못 갔어요.
I couldn't go to school yesterday because of a cold.
mistakes: 비가 때문에 취소했어요.
No particle (이/가, 을/를) may sit between the noun and 때문에; the noun attaches bare.
Say 비 때문에 취소했어요.
친구 때문에 시험에 합격했어요, to express gratitude.
때문에 frames the cause as negative or neutral, so thanking with it sounds odd.
For a welcome cause use 덕분에: 친구 덕분에 합격했어요.

english: because / since V (reason for a request)
formNote: This gives a reason that the speaker is presenting as grounds for what comes next — a request, a suggestion, or a command — so it's the 'since...' that leads into 'so let's / so please.' Add 니까 after a vowel stem (오다 -> 오니까) and 으니까 after a consonant stem (없다 -> 없으니까). Crucial contrast: -(으)니까 vs -아/어서. Use -니까 before an order, request, or suggestion ('비가 오니까 우산을 가져가세요'), but -아/어서 before a plain statement of result and never before a command ('비가 와서 못 갔어요' = 'I couldn't go because it rained'). Also, -아/어서 cannot carry a past-tense marker on its clause, but -니까 can (갔으니까). Pitfall: English speakers default to one 'because' everywhere — saying '늦어서 미안해요' is right, but '늦으니까 미안해요' sounds like you're justifying yourself rather than apologizing, so for apologies and pure cause use -아/어서.
usage: Vowel stem 오다 -> 오니까, leads to a request.
examples: Since it's raining, take an umbrella.
Since I'm busy today, let's meet tomorrow.
제가 벌써 다 봤으니까 이 책 가져가셔도 돼요.
Since I've already read it all, you may take this book.
mistakes: 늦으니까 미안해요.
Before an apology Korean uses -아/어서 (cause), not -니까 (grounds for a request); -니까 makes it sound like an excuse.
Say 늦어서 미안해요.
비가 와니까 우산을 가져가세요.
오다 is a vowel stem, so it's 오니까, not 와니까 — 니까 attaches to the plain stem, not the 아/어 form.
Say 비가 오니까.

formNote: Use this to say one thing resembles or behaves the same way as a noun — 'like / just as.' Attach 처럼 directly to the noun with no particle (가수처럼, 꿈처럼). Sharp contrast: 처럼 expresses likeness or equal degree ('가수처럼 노래해요' = 'sings like a singer'), but 보다 expresses inequality / comparison ('가수보다 잘해요' = 'sings better than a singer'), so they are opposites — one means 'similar to,' the other 'more/less than.' 처럼 also overlaps with 같이 in this sense (가수같이 노래해요 ≈ 가수처럼 노래해요), though 처럼 is the more neutral default. Pitfall: English 'like' doubles as 'such as' for examples, but Korean 처럼 only means 'resembling'; to list examples ('fruits like apples') you'd use 같은 (사과 같은 과일), not 사과처럼 과일.
examples: Today's weather is warm like spring.
저도 한국 사람처럼 자연스럽게 말하고 싶어요.
I want to speak naturally like a Korean person too.
mistakes: 가수처럼 잘해요, when you mean 'better than a singer.'
처럼 means 'as / similar to,' not 'more than'; for surpassing someone use 보다.
Say 가수보다 잘해요 for 'better than.'
사과처럼 과일을 좋아해요, to mean 'fruit such as apples.'
처럼 marks resemblance, not example-listing; this reads 'I like fruit the way I like apples.'
For examples use 같은: 사과 같은 과일을 좋아해요.

english: even if V / even though V
formNote: This concedes a condition that doesn't change the outcome — 'even if / even though.' Build the 아/어 form, then add 도 ('also/even'): use 아 after a bright vowel ㅏ or ㅗ (가다 -> 가도, 오다 -> 와도), 어 otherwise (먹다 -> 먹어도), and 해 for 하다 verbs (공부해도). Contrast with -(으)면 ('if'): -(으)면 says the result depends on the condition ('비가 오면 안 가요' = 'if it rains I won't go'), while -아/어도 says the result holds in spite of it ('비가 와도 가요' = 'even if it rains, I'll go') — so they point in opposite directions. It also overlaps with -지만 ('but'), but -아/어도 is hypothetical ('even if it were') whereas -지만 reports an actual fact ('비싸지만 샀어요' = 'it was expensive but I bought it'). Pitfall: pick the vowel by sound, not by spelling out the stem — 오다 contracts to 와도, never 오아도.
usage: 오다 -> 와도 (ㅗ takes 아, then contracts).
examples: Even if it rains, I'll go.
No matter how busy I am, I exercise every day.
조금 비싸도 품질이 좋으면 이걸 살래요.
Even if it's a bit pricey, if the quality's good I'll buy this.
Concession combined with a 면 condition.
mistakes: 오아도 갈 거예요.
오다 contracts in the 아/어 form to 와, so 오아도 is not a valid spelling.
Say 와도 갈 거예요.
비가 오면 갈 거예요, when you mean 'even if it rains.'
-(으)면 means 'if' (the result depends on it); 'even if / regardless' needs -아/어도.
Say 비가 와도 갈 거예요.

english: while doing V (at the same time)
formNote: Use this when one person does two actions at the same moment — the action in the 면서 clause runs concurrently with the main verb. Add 면서 after a vowel stem (보다 -> 보면서) and 으면서 after a consonant stem (먹다 -> 먹으면서); for ㄷ-irregular verbs the ㄷ becomes ㄹ (듣다 -> 들으면서). Key rule and contrast: the subject of both actions must be the SAME person, which is exactly how -(으)면서 differs from -(으)ㄹ 때 ('when,' which just sets a time and allows different subjects) and from -고 ('and then,' which lets actions be sequential rather than overlapping). 'TV를 보면서 밥을 먹어요' = doing both at once; 'TV를 보고 밥을 먹어요' = watch first, then eat. Pitfall: English 'while' can cover two different people ('while I cooked, he cleaned'), but Korean -(으)면서 cannot — for two separate subjects acting at once use -는 동안 (동안 = 'during') instead.
usage: Stem 마시- ends in a vowel, no 으.
examples: I study while listening to music.
저는 커피를 마시면서 친구하고 천천히 이야기했어요.
I chatted slowly with a friend while drinking coffee.
Past tense lands only on the main verb 이야기했어요.
mistakes: 제가 요리하면서 동생이 청소했어요.
면서 requires one shared subject; here 'I' and 'my sibling' differ, so it's ungrammatical.
For two subjects use 동안: 제가 요리하는 동안 동생이 청소했어요.
듣으면서 공부해요.
듣다 is ㄷ-irregular, so before 으 the ㄷ changes to ㄹ.
Say 들으면서 공부해요.
